# Worth the Fee: full text

> Straight answers on whether a travel card or program is worth it for you.

# Blue Cash Preferred or Blue Cash Everyday: at what grocery spend does the annual fee pay off?

Source: https://itsworththefee.com/amex-blue-cash-preferred-vs-everyday/
Facts checked: 2026-11-20
Publisher: Worth the Fee (independent; some pages end with a disclosed referral link)

The Blue Cash Preferred's $95 annual fee pays off against the no-fee Blue Cash Everyday once you spend more than about $3,167 a year at US supermarkets, which is roughly $264 a month. The most the grocery rate can put you ahead is $85 a year, because the 6% rate stops at $6,000 of grocery spending.

This page is information, not financial advice.

## The two cards side by side

| | Blue Cash Preferred | Blue Cash Everyday |
|---|---|---|
| Annual fee | $0 the first year, then $95 | $0 |
| US supermarkets | 6% on up to $6,000 a year, then 1% | 3% on up to $6,000 a year, then 1% |
| US gas stations | 3% | 3% on up to $6,000 a year, then 1% |
| US online retail | 1% | 3% on up to $6,000 a year, then 1% |
| Select US streaming | 6% | 1% |
| Transit (rideshare, parking, tolls, trains, buses) | 3% | 1% |
| Everything else | 1% | 1% |
| Disney streaming credit | Up to $10 a month ($120 a year) | Up to $7 a month ($84 a year) |
| Foreign transaction fee | 2.7% | 2.7% |

Cash back is paid as Reward Dollars, which can be redeemed as a statement credit. The streaming credit needs enrollment and applies to subscriptions bought at DisneyPlus.com, Hulu.com or Stream.ESPN.com.

## The break-even sum

On groceries, the Preferred earns 6% and the Everyday earns 3%. The difference is 3 cents on each dollar.

$95 fee ÷ 0.03 = $3,166.67 a year

$3,166.67 ÷ 12 = $263.89 a month

Below that amount, the Everyday leaves you with more money. Above it, the Preferred does, up to the cap.

| US supermarket spend per year | Extra cash back from Preferred (3%) | After the $95 fee |
|---|---|---|
| $2,000 (about $167 a month) | $60 | $35 behind |
| $3,167 (about $264 a month) | $95 | Even |
| $4,000 (about $333 a month) | $120 | $25 ahead |
| $5,000 (about $417 a month) | $150 | $55 ahead |
| $6,000 ($500 a month) | $180 | $85 ahead |
| $9,000 ($750 a month) | $180 | $85 ahead |

Past $6,000 both cards earn 1% on groceries, so the gap stops growing.

NerdWallet puts the monthly break-even at $267, slightly above the $264 worked out here. The difference is small and may come from rounding.

In the first year the Preferred has no annual fee, so it is ahead at any grocery spend for those 12 months.

## Things that move the break-even

**Streaming.** The Preferred earns 6% on select US streaming and has a Disney streaming credit that is $36 a year larger. If you already pay for Disney+, Hulu or ESPN and would use the full credit on either card, the fee gap shrinks to $59, and the grocery break-even falls to about $1,967 a year ($59 ÷ 0.03).

**Transit.** The Preferred earns 3% on transit, the Everyday 1%. Each $1,000 of commuting costs adds $20 to the Preferred's side.

**Online shopping.** This goes the other way. The Everyday earns 3% at US online retailers on up to $6,000 a year, and the Preferred earns 1%. Each $1,000 of online shopping is worth $20 more on the Everyday. A household that spends $3,000 a year online gives up $60 by choosing the Preferred, which pushes the grocery break-even up to about $5,167 a year (($95 + $60) ÷ 0.03).

**Gas.** Both earn 3%. The Everyday's rate stops at $6,000 a year; the Preferred's has no stated cap.

## What counts as a US supermarket

Amex's supermarket category covers traditional grocery stores. One Mile at a Time notes that superstores such as Walmart and Target, warehouse clubs such as Costco and Sam's Club, and convenience stores generally do not count. Purchases there earn 1% on either card.

If most of your food shopping is at a superstore or warehouse club, the sums above do not apply to that spending, and the fee will not pay off through groceries.

## Who should skip the Preferred

- Households that spend under about $264 a month at traditional supermarkets and do not use streaming or transit much.
- People who buy groceries mainly at Walmart, Target or Costco.
- People who do more shopping online than in grocery stores.
- People who want a card for travel abroad. Both cards charge a 2.7% foreign transaction fee.

People who want points for travel, not cash back, can compare [the Gold Card's grocery sums](/amex-gold-card-worth-the-fee/).

Welcome offers on both cards vary by applicant and change, and are not part of the sums above.

## Quick answers

**What is the break-even grocery spend?**
About $3,167 a year, or $264 a month, at US supermarkets. That is the $95 fee divided by the 3-point difference in cash back.

**What is the most the Preferred can earn over the Everyday on groceries?**
$85 a year after the fee. The 6% rate applies to the first $6,000 of supermarket spending each year.

**Does Costco count as a supermarket for the 6%?**
No. Warehouse clubs and superstores generally are not counted as US supermarkets.

## Sources

- [CNBC Select: Blue Cash Everyday vs. Blue Cash Preferred](https://www.cnbc.com/select/amex-blue-cash-everyday-vs-preferred/)
- [One Mile at a Time: Blue Cash Preferred review](https://onemileatatime.com/reviews/credit-cards/american-express/blue-cash-preferred-card/)
- [The Points Guy: Blue Cash Preferred vs. Blue Cash Everyday](https://thepointsguy.com/credit-cards/american-express/credit-card-showdown-amex-blue-cash-preferred-vs-everyday/)
- [NerdWallet: Blue Cash Everyday vs. Blue Cash Preferred](https://www.nerdwallet.com/credit-cards/learn/american-express-blue-cash-everyday-vs-blue-cash-preferred-comparison)

# Is the Amex Gold Card worth its annual fee if you cook at home most nights?

Source: https://itsworththefee.com/amex-gold-card-worth-the-fee/
Facts checked: 2026-11-20
Publisher: Worth the Fee (independent; some pages end with a disclosed referral link)

For a home cook the Amex Gold Card can cover its $325 annual fee, but only if you spend a lot at US supermarkets or you would use its monthly credits anyway. On grocery points alone, valued at 1 cent each, it takes about $8,125 of supermarket spending a year to pay the fee back.

This page is information, not financial advice.

## What the card costs and earns

The annual fee is $325. The earning rates that matter in a kitchen:

- 4 points per dollar at US supermarkets, on up to $25,000 per calendar year, then 1 point.
- 4 points per dollar at restaurants worldwide, on up to $50,000 per calendar year, then 1 point.
- 3 points on flights booked with airlines or through Amex Travel, and 1 point on most other purchases.

One limit matters a lot for groceries: superstores and warehouse clubs are not counted as supermarkets. Shopping at Walmart, Target, Costco or Sam's Club earns 1 point, not 4.

## The grocery sum

What 4 points per dollar is worth depends on how you use the points. Covering card charges gives about 0.6 cents per point. Flights through Amex Travel give 1 cent. The Points Guy values a point at 2 cents when moved to airline partners; One Mile at a Time says 1.7 cents. See [what a point is worth by use](/amex-membership-rewards-points-value/).

| Supermarket spend | Points a year | At 0.6 cents | At 1 cent | At 2 cents |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $400 a month ($4,800 a year) | 19,200 | $115 | $192 | $384 |
| $600 a month ($7,200 a year) | 28,800 | $173 | $288 | $576 |
| $800 a month ($9,600 a year) | 38,400 | $230 | $384 | $768 |
| $1,000 a month ($12,000 a year) | 48,000 | $288 | $480 | $960 |

Grocery spend needed to match the $325 fee with no credits used:

- At 0.6 cents per point: about $13,542 a year.
- At 1 cent per point: $8,125 a year, about $677 a month.
- At 2 cents per point: about $4,063 a year, about $339 a month.

## The credits, from a home cook's side

The card has four recurring credits. All need enrollment, and unused amounts are lost each month or half-year.

| Credit | Amount | Where | Useful if you cook at home? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dining | Up to $10 a month ($120 a year) | Grubhub, Buffalo Wild Wings, Five Guys, The Cheesecake Factory, Wonder | Only if you order from one of these each month |
| Uber Cash | Up to $10 a month ($120 a year) | US Uber rides and Uber Eats | Only if you ride or order monthly |
| Resy | Up to $50 each half-year ($100 a year) | US Resy restaurants | Two restaurant meals a year |
| Dunkin' | Up to $7 a month ($84 a year) | US Dunkin' locations | Only if you already buy there |

The four add up to $424 a year on paper. A person who rarely eats out will use much less. An example: if you use the Uber Cash and the Dunkin' credit in full ($204) and nothing else, the fee you still have to earn back is $121. At 1 cent per point that takes about $3,025 of supermarket spending a year, roughly $252 a month.

A credit only counts as money saved if you would have bought the thing anyway.

## Compared with a cash back grocery card

The Blue Cash Preferred, also from Amex, pays 6% cash back at US supermarkets on up to $6,000 a year, for a $95 fee after the first year. On $6,000 of groceries that is $360 in cash. The Gold Card earns 24,000 points on the same spending, worth $144 to $480 depending on use. The [Blue Cash break-even sums are here](/amex-blue-cash-preferred-vs-everyday/).

The Gold Card comes out ahead for a home cook mainly when grocery spending is above $6,000 a year, when points go to airline partners, or when the credits fit existing habits.

## Who should skip it

- People who buy most groceries at Walmart, Target, Costco or another superstore or warehouse club.
- People who spend under about $340 a month at supermarkets and would not use the credits.
- People who want cash back. Used against card charges, points are worth about 0.6 cents each.
- People who will not track four separate credits with monthly or half-year deadlines.
- People who want airport lounge access. This card has none.

Welcome offers on this card vary by applicant and change, and people who have had the card before may not get one. See [the once per lifetime rule](/amex-once-per-lifetime-welcome-offer-rule/).

## Quick answers

**Does Costco or Walmart earn 4 points on the Gold Card?**
No. Superstores and warehouse clubs are not counted as US supermarkets, so they earn 1 point per dollar.

**How much grocery spending covers the $325 fee?**
About $8,125 a year if a point is worth 1 cent to you and you use none of the credits. Less if you use the credits or transfer points to airlines.

**Is there a cap on the 4 points at supermarkets?**
Yes. The 4 points apply to the first $25,000 of US supermarket purchases per calendar year, then 1 point.

## Sources

- [One Mile at a Time: Amex Gold Card review](https://onemileatatime.com/reviews/credit-cards/american-express/amex-gold-card/)
- [The Points Guy: Amex Gold Card review](https://thepointsguy.com/credit-cards/reviews/amex-gold-card-review/)
- [The Points Guy: Amex points value](https://thepointsguy.com/guide/amex-points-value/)
- [CNBC Select: Blue Cash Everyday vs. Blue Cash Preferred](https://www.cnbc.com/select/amex-blue-cash-everyday-vs-preferred/)

# Does the Amex Gold Card have cell phone protection?

Source: https://itsworththefee.com/amex-gold-cell-phone-protection/
Facts checked: 2026-11-23
Publisher: Worth the Fee (independent; some pages end with a disclosed referral link)

No. The consumer American Express Gold Card is not on Amex's list of cards with cell phone protection, and its own benefits page does not show the benefit. What it does have is purchase protection, which can cover a phone bought with the card for the first 90 days.

This page is information, not financial advice.

## What Amex's own list says

Amex keeps a page of the cards that carry cell phone protection. On November 23, 2026 it named 16 cards. The Gold Card was not one of them. The page tells holders of any card not listed to call the number on the back of the card to verify their benefits.

| Listed on Amex's page | Cards |
|---|---|
| Personal | Platinum Card, Centurion Card, Delta SkyMiles Platinum, Delta SkyMiles Reserve, Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant, Hilton Honors Aspire |
| Platinum versions | Charles Schwab, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley |
| Business and corporate | Business Platinum, Business Centurion, Business Gold, Delta SkyMiles Platinum Business, Delta SkyMiles Reserve Business, Corporate Platinum, Corporate Centurion |
| Not listed | American Express Gold Card (consumer) |

The name causes confusion. The American Express Business Gold Card is on the list. The consumer Gold Card is a different product and is not.

## The terms on the cards that have it

Every card on Amex's page links to the same Guide to Benefits.

| Term | Detail |
|---|---|
| Maximum per claim | $800, the lesser of repair cost or replacement value |
| Deductible | $50 per claim |
| Claims | Two per card account per 12-month period |
| Covered events | Theft and damage |
| Condition | The monthly wireless bill is charged to the eligible card |
| Order of payment | After any other insurance that applies |

The full rules, exclusions and claim deadlines are on the page about [Amex Platinum cell phone protection](/amex-platinum-cell-phone-protection/). They come from the same guide.

## Where sources differ

An article from The Points Guy published in March 2021, when the benefit began, lists 12 cards and leaves out several that Amex lists now, including Business Gold. Upgraded Points, updated October 22, 2026, lists Business Gold. No source read for this page says the consumer Gold Card has the benefit.

## What the Gold Card offers instead

Amex's Gold Card page lists these protections. None of them works like phone insurance on a phone you already own.

| Protection | What Amex's page says |
|---|---|
| Purchase protection | Up to 90 days from purchase when an item is accidentally damaged, stolen or lost. Up to $10,000 per purchase and $50,000 per calendar year |
| Extended warranty | Up to one extra year on a manufacturer's warranty of five years or less. Up to $10,000 per item and $50,000 per calendar year |
| Trip delay | Up to $300 per trip after a delay of more than 12 hours, two claims per 12 months |
| Baggage insurance | Up to $1,250 for carry-on and up to $500 for checked baggage |
| Car rental loss and damage | Secondary cover when the rental is paid with the card and the waiver is declined |

Amex's page introduces purchase protection with the words "Dropped your phone?" So a phone bought with the Gold Card has cover for accidental damage, theft or loss in its first 90 days. After that, extended warranty only adds time to the manufacturer's warranty, which deals with defects, not drops or theft.

One source disagrees on the shopping protections. A December 2025 guide from The Points Guy does not list the standard Gold Card for purchase protection or extended warranty. Amex's own Gold Card page lists both.

## The sums

The Gold Card costs $325 a year and the Platinum Card costs $895. Cell phone protection alone does not make up that $570 difference. Compare the [whole set of benefits on each card](/amex-platinum-vs-gold-which-fits/).

For a phone already owned, a Gold cardholder's choices are a carrier or manufacturer protection plan, a homeowner's or renter's policy that applies, or paying the wireless bill with a different card that carries the benefit. The Gold Card earns 1 point per dollar on a wireless bill, so moving that bill gives up little.

## Who should skip counting on it

- Gold cardholders who assumed the phone was covered because the bill is on the card. It is not.
- Anyone who reads "Gold" on Amex's list. That entry is the Business Gold Card.
- Anyone relying on purchase protection for a phone bought more than 90 days ago.
- Anyone weighing the Gold Card mainly on insurance. Its strength is points on restaurants and US supermarkets, covered in [whether the Gold Card is worth its fee](/amex-gold-card-worth-the-fee/).

## Quick answers

**Does the Amex Gold Card have cell phone protection?**
No. The consumer Gold Card is not on Amex's list of eligible cards as of November 23, 2026.

**Does the Amex Business Gold Card have it?**
Yes. Amex lists the Business Gold Card, with up to $800 per claim after a $50 deductible, two claims per 12 months.

**Will the Gold Card cover a new phone I buy with it?**
For 90 days, under purchase protection, if it is accidentally damaged, stolen or lost. Limits are $10,000 per purchase and $50,000 per calendar year.

## Sources

- [American Express: cell phone protection, eligible cards](https://www.americanexpress.com/us/credit-cards/features-benefits/policies/cell-phone-protection.html)
- [American Express: Guide to Benefits, cell phone protection (PDF)](https://www.americanexpress.com/content/dam/amex/us/credit-cards/features-benefits/CPP_GTB_3f1bed_a11y.pdf)
- [American Express: Gold Card](https://www.americanexpress.com/us/credit-cards/card/gold-card/)
- [Upgraded Points: Amex cell phone protection](https://upgradedpoints.com/credit-cards/amex-cell-phone-protection/)
- [The Points Guy: Amex cell phone protection](https://thepointsguy.com/credit-cards/amex-cell-phone-protection/)
- [The Points Guy: American Express shopping protections](https://thepointsguy.com/credit-cards/american-express/american-express-shopping-protections)
- [One Mile at a Time: Amex Gold Card review](https://onemileatatime.com/reviews/credit-cards/american-express/amex-gold-card/)

# Amex Gold or Chase Sapphire Preferred for someone who spends most on food?

Source: https://itsworththefee.com/amex-gold-vs-chase-sapphire-preferred/
Facts checked: 2026-11-20
Publisher: Worth the Fee (independent; some pages end with a disclosed referral link)

The Amex Gold fits a food spender who buys a lot at US supermarkets, because it pays 4 points per dollar there and the Sapphire Preferred pays 1. For someone whose food spending is mostly restaurants, the gap is 1 point per dollar, and the $95 Preferred usually costs less overall.

This page is information, not financial advice. Terms change, so check each issuer's pages before deciding.

## Side by side

| | Amex Gold | Sapphire Preferred |
|---|---|---|
| Annual fee | $325 | $95 |
| Restaurants | 4x worldwide, on up to $50,000 a year | 3x |
| US supermarkets, in store | 4x, on up to $25,000 a year | 1x |
| Online grocery | Not listed separately | 3x, not Walmart, Target or wholesale clubs |
| Flights booked direct | 3x | 2x |
| Gas, EV charging, selected streaming | 1x | 3x |
| Everything else | 1x | 1x |
| Main credits | Up to $424 a year: dining $120, Uber Cash $120, Resy $100, Dunkin' $84 | Up to $100 a year on Chase Travel hotels |
| Airport lounges | None | None |
| Transfer partners | About 16 airlines, Delta included, plus Hilton, Marriott, Choice | 14, including United, Southwest and Hyatt |
| Foreign transaction fee | None | None |

Superstores and warehouse clubs do not count as supermarkets on the Gold. The Gold's credits all need enrollment and run monthly or by half-year.

## The plain sum

The fee gap is $230. The Gold has to return that much more than the Preferred, in points or in credits a reader would have paid cash for.

Extra points on the Gold: 1 per dollar at restaurants, 3 per dollar at supermarkets.

| Yearly food spending | Gold | Preferred | Gold's extra points |
|---|---|---|---|
| $6,000 restaurants, no supermarkets | 24,000 | 18,000 | 6,000 |
| $4,000 restaurants, $4,000 supermarkets | 32,000 | 16,000 | 16,000 |
| $6,000 restaurants, $6,000 supermarkets | 48,000 | 24,000 | 24,000 |
| $6,000 restaurants, $10,000 supermarkets | 64,000 | 28,000 | 36,000 |

What a point is worth depends on how it is used. At 1 cent, 24,000 extra points are $240. One Mile at a Time uses 1.7 cents for points moved to airline partners, which makes them about $408. The Points Guy uses about 2 cents.

Read against the $230 gap:

- **Restaurants only.** 6,000 extra points are worth $60 to $120. The Gold needs about $110 to $170 of its credits, used at face value, to draw level.
- **Restaurants and supermarkets, $12,000 together.** The extra points cover the gap by themselves at 1 cent each.
- **Family grocery bill of $10,000 or more.** The Gold is well ahead before any credit is counted.

## The Gold's credits, counted strictly

| Credit | Amount | Where it works |
|---|---|---|
| Dining | $10 a month | Grubhub, Five Guys, The Cheesecake Factory, Buffalo Wild Wings, Wonder |
| Uber Cash | $10 a month | US Uber rides and Uber Eats |
| Resy | $50 each half-year | US Resy restaurants |
| Dunkin' | $7 a month | US Dunkin' locations |

Someone who already orders from Uber Eats monthly and eats at a Resy restaurant twice a year uses $220 with no change in habits. Someone who uses none of these places should count them as zero. The page on [whether the Gold is worth its fee](/amex-gold-card-worth-the-fee/) has more on each credit.

## What the Preferred does that the Gold does not

- 3x on gas, EV charging and selected streaming.
- Trip cancellation cover up to $10,000 per traveler and primary rental car cover.
- Transfers to United, Southwest and Hyatt (Hyatt at 4 Chase points to 3).
- A fee that is $230 lower every year, with nothing to track.

## Which pattern favors which card

- **Cooks at home, large supermarket bill:** Amex Gold.
- **Eats out often, small grocery bill, uses Uber and Resy anyway:** close; the Gold's credits decide it.
- **Eats out often, uses none of the Gold's credit partners:** Sapphire Preferred.
- **Buys groceries at Walmart, Target or Costco:** neither card pays a bonus there, so the lower fee wins: Sapphire Preferred.
- **Flies Delta on points:** Amex Gold. **Stays at Hyatt or flies United or Southwest on points:** Sapphire Preferred.

## Who should skip both

- Anyone who carries a balance month to month.
- Anyone who wants plain cash back and no points to manage; see [Blue Cash Preferred or Everyday](/amex-blue-cash-preferred-vs-everyday/).
- Anyone with a small food budget. With little spending in the bonus categories, neither fee is covered by points.

Welcome offers on both cards vary by applicant and change. Amex shows its offer before a decision is final; Chase limits each Sapphire bonus to once per person.

## Quick answers

**Which card earns more at restaurants?**
The Gold, 4 points per dollar against 3. On $6,000 a year that is 6,000 more points.

**Does the Sapphire Preferred earn a bonus at the supermarket?**
Only on online grocery orders, at 3x. In-store supermarket purchases earn 1x.

**Do either of these cards get me into airport lounges?**
No. Neither card includes lounge access.

## Sources

- [One Mile at a Time: Amex Gold Card review](https://onemileatatime.com/reviews/credit-cards/american-express/amex-gold-card/)
- [The Points Guy: Amex Gold Card review](https://thepointsguy.com/credit-cards/reviews/amex-gold-card-review/)
- [Chase: Sapphire Preferred card page](https://creditcards.chase.com/rewards-credit-cards/sapphire/preferred)
- [The Points Guy: Chase Sapphire Preferred review](https://thepointsguy.com/credit-cards/chase-sapphire-preferred-review)
- [AwardWallet: Amex transfer partners](https://awardwallet.com/credit-cards/amex-membership-rewards/amex-transfer-partners/)
- [AwardWallet: Chase to Hyatt transfer ratios](https://awardwallet.com/credit-cards/chase-ultimate-rewards/chase-to-hyatt-transfer/)

# What is an Amex Membership Rewards point actually worth?

Source: https://itsworththefee.com/amex-membership-rewards-points-value/
Facts checked: 2026-11-20
Publisher: Worth the Fee (independent; some pages end with a disclosed referral link)

An Amex Membership Rewards point is worth about 0.6 cents when used against card charges, 0.7 cents at shopping checkouts and on most Amex Travel hotels, 1 cent on flights booked through Amex Travel, and roughly 1 to 2 cents or more when moved to an airline partner and used well. The point has no single value; it depends on how you spend it.

This page is information, not financial advice.

## Cents per point by use

| How you use the point | Cents per point | 50,000 points come to | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cover card charges (statement credit) | 0.6 | $300 | The Points Guy, CNBC Select, point.me |
| Pay with Points at Amazon and similar checkouts | 0.7 | $350 | CNBC Select, The Points Guy |
| Gift cards | 0.5 to 1.0, by brand | $250 to $500 | The Points Guy, CNBC Select |
| Amex Travel: most prepaid hotels, rental cars | About 0.7 | $350 | The Points Guy, CNBC Select |
| Amex Travel: cruises | 0.5 to 0.7 | $250 to $350 | The Points Guy |
| Amex Travel: flights | 1.0 | $500 | The Points Guy, CNBC Select |
| Amex Travel: Fine Hotels + Resorts (Platinum cards only) | 1.0 | $500 | The Points Guy, CNBC Select |
| Transfer to an airline or hotel partner | Varies; valued at 1.7 to 2.0 on average | $850 to $1,000 | One Mile at a Time, The Points Guy |

## Where sources disagree

**Gift cards.** The Points Guy gives a range of 0.5 to 1 cent. CNBC Select says gift cards are generally 1 cent, with some brands at 0.7 or 0.85 cents and American Express gift cards at 0.5 cents. point.me gives about 0.7 cents. The rate is set brand by brand, so check the points price of the exact card.

**Transfer partners.** This is an estimate, not a rate. The Points Guy values a point at 2.0 cents (April 2026). One Mile at a Time says 1.7 cents. point.me says about 1.7 cents for a standard transfer and 3 to 5 cents for premium-cabin awards. CNBC Select notes that transfers to Marriott Bonvoy and Choice Privileges are typically under 1 cent, and that Delta SkyMiles average about 1.2 cents.

**Number of partners.** CNBC Select counts 21 (18 airlines and 3 hotel programs). point.me counts 20. The list changes.

## How transfers work

Most partners take points at 1 to 1. Some differ:

| Partner | Ratio (Amex points to partner points) |
|---|---|
| Most airline partners | 1 : 1 |
| Hilton Honors | 1 : 2 |
| Aeromexico Rewards | 1 : 1.6 |
| Cathay Pacific, Emirates Skywards | 5 : 4 |
| JetBlue TrueBlue | 250 : 200 |

A higher ratio does not mean higher value. Two Hilton points at The Points Guy's 0.4 cents each come to 0.8 cents per Amex point.

Transfers to US airlines carry a fee. Thrifty Traveler and point.me give it as $0.0006 per point (0.06 cents), capped at $99, on transfers to Delta and JetBlue. That is $30 on 50,000 points. The Points Guy and CNBC Select print larger per-point figures (0.6 and 0.5 cents), which do not fit the $99 cap; the fee shown on Amex's transfer screen is the one that applies.

A transfer partner value above 1 cent exists only if you find an award seat you would have paid cash for.

## A worked example

Take the 24,000 points that $6,000 of supermarket spending earns on [the Gold Card](/amex-gold-card-worth-the-fee/):

- As a statement credit: $144.
- As a flight through Amex Travel: $240.
- Moved to an airline at 1.7 cents: $408, if a suitable award is found.

The same points are worth almost three times as much at the top of that list as at the bottom.

## Which number to use for your own sums

- If you would take cash or a statement credit, use 0.6 cents.
- If you would book flights through Amex Travel, use 1 cent.
- If you already book award flights through airline programs and have flexible dates, the published valuations of 1.7 to 2 cents are the figures to test. They are not guaranteed.

Published valuations describe what an experienced user can get. They are not a cash price.

## Who should skip a Membership Rewards card

- People who want cash back. At 0.6 cents per point, a card that earns 4 points per dollar returns 2.4%, and a card that earns 1 point returns 0.6%.
- People who will not learn an airline program or search for award seats.
- People with fixed travel dates and one home airline that is not a transfer partner.
- People who would mostly redeem for gift cards or checkout purchases.

Points can also come from shopping portals; see [Rakuten paid in Amex points](/rakuten-amex-points-instead-of-cash/).

## Quick answers

**What is the cash value of an Amex point?**
About 0.6 cents when used to cover card charges, according to The Points Guy, CNBC Select and point.me.

**Is a point really worth 2 cents?**
Only as an estimate for transfers to travel partners. The Points Guy uses 2.0 cents and One Mile at a Time 1.7 cents. Most other uses give 1 cent or less.

**Is there a fee to transfer points to an airline?**
For US airlines such as Delta and JetBlue, yes. Thrifty Traveler gives it as 0.06 cents per point, up to $99.

# What is the Amex "once per lifetime" welcome offer rule, and how do you know if you are still eligible?

Source: https://itsworththefee.com/amex-once-per-lifetime-welcome-offer-rule/
Facts checked: 2026-11-20
Publisher: Worth the Fee (independent; some pages end with a disclosed referral link)

The "once per lifetime" rule means American Express generally gives the welcome offer on a card only once per person: if you have or have had that card, you may not get the offer again. You find out for certain during the application, where Amex shows a notice if no welcome offer is available to you and lets you withdraw before the application is processed.

This page is information, not financial advice.

## What the terms say

The Points Guy reports that the current Platinum Card terms say "you may not be eligible to receive a welcome offer" if you have or have had the card.

Two things to know about that wording:

- It is about one card at a time. Having had the Gold Card does not, by this sentence alone, affect a Delta or Hilton card.
- It says "may not". AwardWallet reported in October 2025 that Amex had changed the sentence from a flat statement that the offer was not available to past and current cardholders to this softer form. Whether Amex applies the rule more loosely now is not confirmed.

## What counts as "this Card"

| Situation | Does it count as having had the card? |
|---|---|
| You held the card and closed it years ago | Yes |
| The card was renamed (for example, Premier Rewards Gold became the Gold Card) | Yes |
| You got the card by upgrading from another Amex card | Yes |
| You hold the business version and apply for the personal version | No, they are separate cards |
| You are an authorized user on someone else's card | No, you can still get the offer on your own account |

Amex's terms also list other things it may weigh: your history with balance transfers, your history as a cardmember, and how many cards you have opened and closed.

## Card-family rules

On some cards the terms go further and name other cards in the same family. Holding or having held a higher card can block the offer on a lower one.

| Applying for | Cards that can make you ineligible | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Gold Card | The Gold Card, and any version of the Platinum Card (including the Schwab and Morgan Stanley versions) | Upgraded Points, The Points Guy |
| Green Card | Green, Gold and Platinum cards and earlier versions (rule added in 2024; Upgraded Points reports the card is now closed to new applicants) | AwardWallet |
| Delta SkyMiles Gold | Delta Gold, Platinum and Reserve and earlier versions | The Points Guy |
| Delta SkyMiles Platinum | Delta Platinum and Reserve | The Points Guy |

The rule runs one way. The Points Guy notes that someone who wants both the Gold and Platinum offers would need the Gold first. For Delta, the family rule covers personal cards; business cards are outside it.

Family rules for the Hilton, Marriott and Blue Cash cards are not confirmed in the sources read for this page. Read the offer terms on the application for the exact list.

## The pop-up notice

The confirmed part: Amex tells you before processing the application if you are not eligible for the welcome offer.

- A notice can appear during the application saying you may be approved for the card but will not get the welcome offer. Upgraded Points gives the message as stating that no welcome offer is available to you at this time.
- You then choose to withdraw or to go on without the offer.
- Upgraded Points reports the notice comes before a hard credit inquiry, so withdrawing does not affect your credit score.
- The Points Guy adds that a similar message can show while you browse Amex cards, and that Amex has a welcome offer eligibility tool.

## How to check before you apply

1. List every Amex card you have held, including closed ones and earlier names of the same card.
2. Read the "offer terms" on the application page. Look for the eligibility sentence and the cards it names.
3. Go through the application up to the offer screen. On cards with "as high as" offers, Amex shows your offer amount there. More on that in [how Amex referral offers work](/amex-referral-offer-how-it-works/).
4. If a notice says there is no welcome offer for you, decide whether the card is worth holding without one.

## What is not confirmed

- **A seven-year reset.** A common belief is that "lifetime" ends about seven years after you close a card. One Mile at a Time says Amex has not confirmed this. Do not plan on it.
- **Targeted offers.** Amex sometimes sends offers by mail, email or in your account without the lifetime sentence. These depend on being targeted and cannot be requested.

## Who should skip a new application

- People who had the same card before and are applying mainly for the welcome offer.
- People who hold or held a higher card in the same family, where the terms name it.
- People who see the no-offer notice and would not want the card on its benefits alone.

Welcome offer amounts vary by applicant and change. Nothing here promises one.

## Quick answers

**Can I get an Amex welcome offer twice on the same card?**
Generally no. The terms say you may not be eligible if you have or have had the card.

**Will Amex tell me before a credit check?**
The terms say Amex notifies you before processing the application. Upgraded Points reports the notice appears before a hard inquiry.

**Does having the Platinum Card block the Gold Card offer?**
It can. The Gold Card terms name the Platinum Card as a reason you may not be eligible.

## Sources

- [The Points Guy: Amex welcome offer lifetime restrictions](https://thepointsguy.com/credit-cards/american-express-bonus-lifetime-restrictions/)
- [One Mile at a Time: Amex "once in a lifetime" rule](https://onemileatatime.com/guides/amex-lifetime-rule/)
- [Upgraded Points: Amex Gold welcome offer eligibility](https://upgradedpoints.com/credit-cards/reviews/american-express-gold-card/welcome-offer-eligibility-changes/)
- [AwardWallet: Changes to the once-per-lifetime wording](https://awardwallet.com/news/amex-membership-rewards/amex-once-per-lifetime-rule-changes/)
- [AwardWallet: Family restrictions on the Green Card](https://awardwallet.com/news/credit-cards/amex-adds-family-restrictions-green-card/)
- [The Points Guy: Delta Amex offers and eligibility](https://thepointsguy.com/credit-cards/delta-amex-current-offers/)
- [One Mile at a Time: Amex Platinum welcome offer](https://onemileatatime.com/reviews/credit-cards/american-express/amex-platinum-card-bonus/)

# What does the Amex Platinum $200 airline fee credit actually cover?

Source: https://itsworththefee.com/amex-platinum-airline-fee-credit-what-counts/
Facts checked: 2026-11-20
Publisher: Worth the Fee (independent; some pages end with a disclosed referral link)

It covers incidental fees, such as checked bags, seat selection and in-flight food, on one airline you choose in advance, up to $200 per calendar year. It does not cover airline tickets, award tickets, upgrades, miles or gift cards.

This page is information, not financial advice.

## The rules in short

| Rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| Amount | Up to $200 per calendar year, January 1 to December 31 |
| Rollover | None |
| Airline | One, chosen in your Amex account before you pay the fee |
| Changing airline | Once a year, in January. Last year's choice carries over if you do nothing |
| How it pays | A statement credit, within 8 weeks under the terms; often sooner |
| Additional cards | Their fees on the same airline count toward the one $200 |

You get back only what you spend on eligible fees. Someone who pays $70 in bag fees in a year gets $70.

## Which airlines you can pick

Sources do not agree on the current list.

| Airline | AwardWallet (May 2026) | The Points Guy (July 2026) |
|---|---|---|
| Alaska | Yes | Yes |
| American | Yes | Yes |
| Delta | Yes | Yes |
| JetBlue | Yes | Yes |
| Southwest | Yes | Yes |
| United | Yes | Yes |
| Hawaiian | Removed after its merger with Alaska | Still listed |
| Spirit | Removed after it stopped flying in May 2026 | Not listed |

The six airlines both sources list are safe to assume. Amex says the list can change, so the selection screen in your own account is the final word.

## What counts

The Points Guy and AwardWallet list these as generally eligible, when the airline charges them separately from the ticket:

- Checked bag fees, including overweight and oversized bags
- Seat assignment fees
- Change fees
- In-flight food and drinks
- In-flight entertainment charged by the airline
- Pet fees
- Phone booking fees
- Airport lounge day passes and annual lounge memberships

## What does not count

- Airline tickets
- Award tickets
- Upgrades
- Buying or transferring miles
- Gift cards
- Duty-free purchases
- In-flight Wi-Fi billed by an outside provider
- Fees charged by a partner airline, even on a trip booked through your chosen airline
- Fees charged before you selected the airline
- A seat fee paid in the same charge as the ticket

On taxes and fees for award tickets, sources disagree. One Mile at a Time lists award ticket fees as often refunded. AwardWallet lists them as not counting, and The Points Guy calls them unofficial and unreliable. Do not plan around them.

## Why a fee that should count sometimes does not

Amex does not review each charge by hand. It relies on how the airline labels the transaction. If a fee is labeled as airfare, no credit arrives. The Points Guy notes that United lounge passes may be labeled this way. If a fee you believe qualifies has not been credited after 8 weeks, the terms say to call the number on the back of the card.

## Older workarounds

Some cardholders once used the credit on United TravelBank funds or small Delta gift cards. Upgraded Points reports that these stopped working in early 2026. That is one source, so it is not confirmed.

## What it is worth to you

Work it out from fees you already pay on one airline in a year.

| Your flying | Likely yearly value |
|---|---|
| A family checking bags on the same airline several times a year | Up to $200 |
| Two round trips, one checked bag each way | Four bag fees at your airline's price |
| Carry-on only, no paid seats | $0 |
| Free bags already, through airline status or an airline card | Little, unless you pay for seats or lounge passes |

Bag prices vary by airline and route; check your airline's current fee.

## Who should skip it

Leave this credit out of your sums on the $895 fee if:

- You travel with a carry-on and take whatever seat is assigned.
- You already get free checked bags on the airline you fly most.
- You mostly fly airlines that are not on the list, including all foreign airlines.
- You expected it to reduce the price of a ticket. It will not.

For the other credits, see [what the credits are worth](/amex-platinum-credits-real-value/). For light travelers, see [the occasional flyer page](/amex-platinum-worth-it-occasional-flyer/).

## Quick answers

**Does the Amex Platinum airline credit cover plane tickets?**
No. Tickets, award tickets and upgrades are excluded. It covers extra fees such as checked bags.

**Can you change your selected airline during the year?**
The rule is once a year, in January. The Points Guy reports Amex has sometimes allowed a later change, but that is not guaranteed.

**Does the unused part carry over to next year?**
No. The credit resets on January 1 and anything unused on December 31 is lost.

## Sources

- [AwardWallet: Amex Platinum airline fee credit](https://awardwallet.com/blog/amex-platinum-airline-fee-credit)
- [The Points Guy: choosing your airline for the fee credit](https://thepointsguy.com/credit-cards/american-express/choosing-your-amex-platinum-200-airline-fee-credit/)
- [One Mile at a Time: Amex airline fee credits](https://onemileatatime.com/guides/amex-airline-fee-credits/)
- [The Points Guy: Spirit and the Amex airline benefit](https://thepointsguy.com/news/amex-airline-benefit-spirit/)
- [Upgraded Points: Amex Platinum benefits](https://upgradedpoints.com/credit-cards/reviews/american-express-platinum-card/benefits/)
- [American Express: the airline fee credit](https://www.americanexpress.com/en-us/credit-cards/credit-intel/using-your-american-express-platinum-airline-credit/)

# When is the Amex Platinum annual fee charged, and can you get it refunded?

Source: https://itsworththefee.com/amex-platinum-annual-fee-when-charged-and-refund/
Facts checked: 2026-11-22
Publisher: Worth the Fee (independent; some pages end with a disclosed referral link)

The $895 annual fee is reported to post on your first billing statement and then once every 12 statements. Amex's cardmember agreement says the fee is refunded if you close the account within 30 days after the closing date of the statement that shows it. After that, the fee is non-refundable.

This page is information, not financial advice.

## When the fee posts

Amex's agreement does not give a posting date. Doctor of Credit's guide to issuer fee timing reports this pattern for Amex:

| Year | When the fee posts |
|---|---|
| First year | The first statement closing date after approval |
| Later years | Every twelfth statement after that: the 13th, the 25th and so on |

This timing comes from one source and was not confirmed on a US Amex page.

The fee is due with that statement's balance. It does not count toward a welcome offer's spending requirement, because a fee is not a purchase. See [what counts toward the spending requirement](/amex-platinum-welcome-offer-spending-requirement/).

## The refund rule, in Amex's words

The Platinum Card agreement says Amex will refund the annual fee if you tell it you are voluntarily closing the account within 30 days after the closing date of the billing statement on which the fee appears. It goes on: "For cancellations after this 30-day period, the Annual Fee is non-refundable."

The clock starts at the statement closing date, not the payment due date.

| Example | Date |
|---|---|
| Statement showing the fee closes | January 10 |
| Last day to close for a full refund | February 9 |
| Closing on February 10 or later | No refund |

Two details from the agreement:

- The rule covers closing by your own choice, by calling or writing to Amex.
- The agreement says this policy does not apply if your billing address is in Massachusetts when you close. What applies there is not confirmed.

**Where sources differ.** One Mile at a Time (September 2026) describes the window as 30 days from the fee being billed. The Points Guy and Doctor of Credit count 30 days after the statement. This page uses the agreement's wording.

## Downgrading instead of closing

The agreement's refund rule covers closing only. One Mile at a Time, The Points Guy and Doctor of Credit report that a downgrade after the 30 days often brings a prorated refund of the unused fee. That is not confirmed in an Amex document. The choices, their fees and what happens to your points are on [the downgrade and cancel page](/amex-platinum-downgrade-or-cancel-options/).

## Additional card fees

| Card | Yearly fee |
|---|---|
| Each Additional Platinum Card | $195 |
| Each Companion Platinum Card | $0 |

The agreement applies the same refund policy to an additional card's fee: the 30 days run from the closing date of the statement showing that fee, and the policy applies when you cancel that additional card. When the $195 posts, and whether it follows the main card's date or the date the additional card was added, is not confirmed. See [whether an additional card is worth $195](/amex-platinum-authorized-user-worth-195/).

## Closing in the first year

The Points Guy (2020) and One Mile at a Time (2017) quote Amex welcome offer terms that name canceling or downgrading within 12 months of opening as a reason Amex may withhold or take back welcome points, and may close your other Amex accounts. The current Platinum Card offer terms could not be read for this page, so whether today's offer carries that wording is not confirmed.

A new cardholder who closes inside the first 30-day window gets the fee back under the agreement but falls inside the 12-month wording. Welcome offers vary by applicant and change; see [the once-per-lifetime rule](/amex-once-per-lifetime-welcome-offer-rule/).

## The sums at renewal

| If you | Fee outcome |
|---|---|
| Close within 30 days after the renewal statement closes | $895 refunded |
| Close after that | $0 refunded |
| Downgrade after that | Prorated refund reported, not confirmed by Amex |

Before the window ends, count what the [credits](/amex-platinum-credits-real-value/) returned over the past year.

## Who should skip relying on a refund

- Anyone past the 30 days. The agreement says the fee stays paid.
- Anyone in the first 12 months who cares about the welcome points.
- Anyone whose only Membership Rewards card is the Platinum and who still holds points.
- Anyone counting on a prorated refund for a downgrade without hearing the amount from Amex.

## Quick answers

**When does Amex charge the Platinum annual fee?**
Doctor of Credit reports it posts on the first statement after approval, then on every twelfth statement after that.

**How long do I have to cancel and get the annual fee back?**
Thirty days after the closing date of the statement that shows the fee, under Amex's cardmember agreement.

**Does the annual fee count toward the welcome offer spending?**
No. Fees are not purchases, so the $895 does not count.

## Sources

- [American Express: Platinum Card cardmember agreement (PDF)](https://www.americanexpress.com/content/dam/amex/en-us/company/legal/cardmember-agreements/public-site-adhoc-2025-09-18/platinum-card-09-18-2025.pdf)
- [Doctor of Credit: when issuers charge annual fees](https://www.doctorofcredit.com/issuers-charge-annual-fees-guide/)
- [Doctor of Credit: annual fee refund rules by issuer](https://www.doctorofcredit.com/annual-fee-refund-rules-for-each-card-issuer/)
- [One Mile at a Time: credit card annual fee refund rules](https://onemileatatime.com/?p=325172)
- [The Points Guy: keeping a new Amex account open at least one year](https://thepointsguy.com/credit-cards/american-express/keep-new-amex-account-open-at-least-one-year/)
- [One Mile at a Time: Amex welcome offer terms wording](https://onemileatatime.com/amex-adds-strong-language-to-counter-bonus-abuse/)

# What credit score and income do you need for the Amex Platinum?

Source: https://itsworththefee.com/amex-platinum-approval-requirements/
Facts checked: 2026-11-21
Publisher: Worth the Fee (independent; some pages end with a disclosed referral link)

American Express publishes no minimum credit score and no minimum income for the Platinum Card. Guides describe the usual applicant as having good to excellent credit, and Amex's "Apply With Confidence" process can tell a new applicant whether they are approved before any hard inquiry is placed on their credit report.

This page is information, not financial advice.

## What Amex says, and what guides say

Upgraded Points puts it plainly: "American Express does not disclose a minimum credit score requirement." The numbers below are estimates from review sites, not rules.

| Source | Credit score | Income |
|---|---|---|
| American Express | No minimum published | No minimum published |
| Upgraded Points (July 2026) | FICO 670 or higher can improve the chances | $50,000 or more may improve the odds |
| CNBC Select (November 2026) | Good to excellent; no number given | No number; higher income helps |
| Other sites seen in search results | 690 and 720 | Not given |

The sources disagree on a number, and none of them is the issuer. CNBC Select notes that good credit does not guarantee approval.

## What else Amex looks at

A score is one input. Guides and Amex's own card agreement name others:

- Income and the resources Amex knows about.
- Your history with Amex, if you have other Amex cards.
- How many cards you have open and how recently you opened them.
- Your payment history and balances on other accounts.

The Platinum Card has no preset spending limit, so there is no fixed credit line to qualify for. The annual fee is $895.

Amex can check any of the three credit bureaus. Upgraded Points says applicants most often report Experian.

## How the pre-approval notice works

Amex calls it Apply With Confidence. The steps, as described by Bankrate and The Points Guy:

1. You fill in the normal application: name, address, income, Social Security number.
2. A notice on the form says you can learn whether you are approved with no effect on your credit score.
3. You submit. Amex runs a soft check, which does not change your score.
4. Amex answers yes or no. If yes, it shows the welcome offer attached to the approval.
5. You choose. If you accept the card, Amex then submits a hard inquiry. If you walk away, no hard inquiry is made.

For the Platinum Card, One Mile at a Time describes the same order in November 2026: Amex shows your offer first, and no hard inquiry happens unless you accept.

### Limits of the notice

| Situation | What happens |
|---|---|
| New to Amex, applying for a personal card | The notice is offered |
| Logged in to an existing Amex account | Not offered, per The Points Guy and One Mile at a Time |
| Existing Amex cardholder | Not needed in most cases; Amex generally does not run a hard inquiry on current customers, per Bankrate and The Points Guy |
| Business cards | Not offered |

Accepting the card still has an effect. Upgraded Points says the hard inquiry can lower a score by a few points for a time. For what that does to a score, see [does applying for a travel card hurt your credit score](/does-applying-for-a-travel-card-hurt-credit-score/).

Whether Amex can still decline an application after you accept is not confirmed. No source read addresses it.

## Approval is not the same as the welcome offer

Two separate things are decided: whether you get the card, and whether you get a welcome offer.

- Welcome offers vary by applicant and change over time. The amount you are shown may differ from the highest advertised figure.
- Amex generally gives a welcome offer on a given card once per lifetime. A pop-up during the application tells you if you are not eligible for the offer, and you can stop there. See [the once-per-lifetime rule](/amex-once-per-lifetime-welcome-offer-rule/).
- For ways to see your own offer before deciding, see [how to check your Platinum offer](/highest-amex-platinum-welcome-offer-how-to-check/).

## If you are declined

CNBC Select says a declined applicant can call Amex and ask for the decision to be reconsidered. Upgraded Points suggests checking your credit reports for errors, paying down balances and building a longer history before trying again.

## Who should skip it

Hold off on this card for now if:

- You are new to credit or have had a credit card for under a year.
- You have recent late payments or high balances on other cards.
- A hard inquiry would matter soon, for example before a mortgage application.
- Paying an $895 annual fee would strain your budget.

Whether the card is worth its fee is a separate question from whether you would be approved. See [what the credits are worth](/amex-platinum-credits-real-value/).

## Quick answers

**What is the minimum credit score for the Amex Platinum?**
Amex does not publish one. Review sites suggest good to excellent credit, with estimates from 670 to 720.

**Is there a minimum income for the Amex Platinum?**
None is published. One guide says $50,000 or more may help, but that is an estimate, not an Amex rule.

**Does checking for approval with Amex cause a hard inquiry?**
Not under Apply With Confidence. Amex runs a soft check first, and a hard inquiry follows only if you accept the card.

## Sources

- [Upgraded Points: Amex Platinum credit score requirements](https://upgradedpoints.com/credit-cards/reviews/american-express-platinum-card/credit-score-requirements/)
- [CNBC Select: Amex Platinum credit score](https://www.cnbc.com/select/amex-platinum-credit-score/)
- [Bankrate: Amex Apply With Confidence](https://www.bankrate.com/credit-cards/issuers/amex-apply-with-confidence/)
- [The Points Guy: American Express Apply With Confidence](https://thepointsguy.com/guide/american-express-apply-with-confidence)
- [One Mile at a Time: Amex Apply With Confidence](https://onemileatatime.com/news/amex-apply-with-confidence/)

- [American Express: Platinum Card Member Agreement](https://www.americanexpress.com/content/dam/amex/en-us/company/legal/cardmember-agreements/public-site-adhoc-2025-09-18/platinum-card-09-18-2025.pdf)

# Is adding an authorized user to the Amex Platinum worth $195?

Source: https://itsworththefee.com/amex-platinum-authorized-user-worth-195/
Facts checked: 2026-11-20
Publisher: Worth the Fee (independent; some pages end with a disclosed referral link)

It is worth $195 a year mainly for someone who will use airport lounges, either with you about four or more times a year or alone. The additional cardholder gets lounge access and hotel and car rental status, but not a second set of the statement credits.

This page is information, not financial advice.

## What it costs

Each additional Platinum card costs $195 a year, on top of the primary card's $895 fee. Until September 2025 the price was $175 for up to three cards together, so adding several people is now much more expensive than it was.

## What the additional cardholder gets

| Benefit | Detail |
|---|---|
| Centurion Lounges | Their own entry, with you or alone |
| Delta Sky Club | Their own 10 visits a year, on a same-day Delta flight |
| Priority Pass Select | Their own membership; The Points Guy says they must enroll by phone |
| Plaza Premium lounges | Included |
| Hotel status | Hilton Honors Gold and Marriott Bonvoy Gold, after enrolling |
| Leading Hotels of the World | Leaders Club Sterling status |
| Car rental status | Hertz President's Circle, Avis Preferred Plus, National Emerald Club Executive |
| Global Entry or TSA PreCheck | Their own fee credit, up to $120 or up to $85, once every four years |
| Hotel programs | Can book Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection |

## What they do not get

| Benefit | Why not |
|---|---|
| Uber Cash ($200) | Goes only to the primary cardholder |
| Hotel credit ($600) | One per account |
| Resy credit ($400) | One per account |
| Digital entertainment credit ($300) | One per account |
| lululemon, Equinox, CLEAR+, Walmart+, Uber One credits | One per account |
| Airline fee credit ($200) | One per account |
| A welcome offer | One per account |

For the shared credits, a purchase on the additional card can use up the account's credit. It does not create a new one. The additional card's spending earns points into the primary cardholder's account and counts toward the primary's welcome offer spending.

## The sum for a couple

Without an additional card, a partner enters a Centurion Lounge as your guest at $50 a visit, and must be on your flight. The Delta Sky Club guest fee is also charged per visit; sources put it at $50 or $29.

| Centurion visits together per year | Guest fees | Additional card |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | $100 | $195 |
| 3 | $150 | $195 |
| 4 | $200 | $195 |

Below four visits a year, paying the guest fee costs less.

Three things can move the sum:

- **Traveling alone.** A guest cannot enter without you. If your partner flies alone, only their own card gets them in. For them the comparison is $195 against whatever they would pay for lounges otherwise.
- **Priority Pass.** Your own Priority Pass already allows two free guests where the lounge takes guests. If those are the lounges you use together, the additional card saves nothing there.
- **The one-time credit.** In a year when the additional cardholder pays for Global Entry, up to $120 comes back, which leaves $75 for that year.

## The no-fee Companion Card

Amex also offers a Companion Platinum Card with no annual fee. The Points Guy describes its benefits as very limited, and it does not include lounge access. It suits someone who only needs a card on the account for spending. The benefits in the table above belong to the $195 card only.

## Who can be added

The Points Guy gives a minimum age of 13. The maximum number of additional Platinum cards on one account is not confirmed.

An additional cardholder who later wants their own Platinum account can still be eligible for a welcome offer on it, according to One Mile at a Time. Offers vary by applicant and change.

## Who should skip it

Adding a $195 card is hard to justify if:

- The person flies once or twice a year. Guest fees for those trips cost less.
- You expected a second set of credits. There is none.
- Your airports have Priority Pass lounges but no Centurion Lounge or Delta Sky Club.
- You are adding children mainly for lounges. Compare with the child guest fee of $30 a visit first; see [the guest rules page](/amex-platinum-centurion-lounge-guest-rules/).

If the primary card itself is a close call, start with [what the credits are worth](/amex-platinum-credits-real-value/).

## Quick answers

**How much is an authorized user on the Amex Platinum?**
$195 a year for each additional Platinum card. A Companion Platinum Card has no fee but very limited benefits.

**Do authorized users get their own Uber Cash and statement credits?**
No. Uber Cash goes to the primary cardholder only, and the other credits are one per account.

**Do authorized users get Centurion Lounge access?**
Yes, with the $195 additional Platinum card. The no-fee Companion card does not include lounge access.

# What does Amex Platinum cell phone protection cover, and what is the deductible?

Source: https://itsworththefee.com/amex-platinum-cell-phone-protection/
Facts checked: 2026-11-23
Publisher: Worth the Fee (independent; some pages end with a disclosed referral link)

It covers the cost to repair or replace a stolen or damaged phone, including a cracked screen, up to $800 per claim after a $50 deductible, with two claims per 12 months. The wireless bill must be paid with the card. A lost phone is not covered, and the benefit pays only what other insurance does not.

This page is information, not financial advice.

## The terms at a glance

These come from Amex's Guide to Benefits for cell phone protection, which names the Platinum Card as an eligible account.

| Term | Detail |
|---|---|
| Maximum per claim | $800, the lesser of repair cost or replacement value |
| Deductible | $50 per claim |
| Claims | Two per card account per 12-month period |
| Covered events | Theft and damage, including a cracked screen |
| Which phones | The primary line and additional lines on your wireless bill |
| Underwriter | New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG company |

The deductible is taken from the repair or replacement cost first, and the $800 cap applies after that. A $300 screen repair pays $250. A $1,200 replacement pays $800.

## How to have cover in place

Charge your monthly wireless bill to the Platinum Card. Cover starts on the first day of the calendar month after that payment.

If a month's bill is paid another way, cover is suspended from the first day of the following month. It resumes the first day of the month after you next pay the bill with the card.

Additional card members count as card members under the guide.

## What it does not cover

- **Lost phones.** A phone that is lost, or that vanishes without evidence of theft, is excluded.
- **Cosmetic damage.** Scratches, scuffs and chips that do not break through the screen or casing and do not affect how the phone works. A cracked screen is not treated as cosmetic.
- **Accessories.** Only the standard battery and antenna from the manufacturer are included.
- **Phones in transit.** A phone in the care of the mail, an airline or a delivery service.
- **Rented, leased, borrowed or prepaid-plan phones.**
- **Phones bought for resale or for commercial use**, on consumer cards.
- **Wear, defects and disasters.** Normal wear and tear, product defects, flood and earthquake.
- **Warranty losses.** Anything a manufacturer or seller warranty covers.

## It pays after other insurance

The guide calls the cover "excess of any other applicable insurance or indemnity." If you have phone insurance through your carrier, or a homeowner's or renter's policy that applies, the card benefit pays only what those do not. Claim papers can include a copy of the claim you made to that insurer, or the policy's declarations page if the loss is under its deductible.

## Filing a claim

| Step | Deadline |
|---|---|
| Report the loss by phone or on the claims website | Within 90 days of the loss |
| Send written proof | Within 120 days of the loss |
| Police report, for theft | Filed within 48 hours of the theft |

Papers include the card statement showing the phone bill payment, the wireless bill, proof of the phone model, and a repair estimate with photos.

## The sums

If the benefit lets you drop a paid protection plan, the saving is that plan's monthly fee times 12, per line. Weigh three things against it:

- The benefit excludes loss, which paid plans often include.
- The $800 cap is below the price of many flagship phones.
- Upgraded Points notes the phone bill generally earns 1 point per dollar on premium Amex cards. A card that pays more on phone bills, or a carrier discount for paying another way, is what you give up.

This benefit alone does not carry an $895 annual fee. It is one line in the [full count of what the card returns](/amex-platinum-credits-real-value/).

The benefit does not come with every Amex card. The consumer Gold Card is not on the list; see [whether the Amex Gold has cell phone protection](/amex-gold-cell-phone-protection/).

## Who should skip relying on it

- Anyone mainly worried about losing a phone. Loss is excluded.
- Anyone with a phone worth well over $800 who wants full replacement.
- Anyone on a prepaid plan or with a leased phone.
- Anyone who will not keep the wireless bill on this card every month.

## Quick answers

**What is the deductible on Amex Platinum cell phone protection?**
$50 per claim. It is applied to the repair or replacement cost before the $800 cap.

**Does it cover a cracked screen?**
Yes. The guide lists a cracked screen as covered damage and says it is not cosmetic damage.

**Does it cover a lost phone?**
No. Lost phones and unexplained disappearance are excluded. Theft is covered with a police report filed within 48 hours.

## Sources

- [American Express: Guide to Benefits, cell phone protection (PDF)](https://www.americanexpress.com/content/dam/amex/us/credit-cards/features-benefits/CPP_GTB_3f1bed_a11y.pdf)
- [Upgraded Points: Amex cell phone protection](https://upgradedpoints.com/credit-cards/amex-cell-phone-protection/)
- [The Points Guy: Amex cell phone protection](https://thepointsguy.com/credit-cards/amex-cell-phone-protection/)

# Can you bring guests into a Centurion Lounge with the Amex Platinum, and what does it cost?

Source: https://itsworththefee.com/amex-platinum-centurion-lounge-guest-rules/
Facts checked: 2026-11-20
Publisher: Worth the Fee (independent; some pages end with a disclosed referral link)

Yes. A Platinum cardholder can bring up to two guests into a US Centurion Lounge, but each adult guest costs $50 and each child costs $30. Guests are free only after you put $75,000 of eligible purchases on the card in a calendar year.

This page is information, not financial advice.

## Guest prices at US Centurion Lounges

| Guest | Price per visit |
|---|---|
| Adult, 18 or older | $50 |
| Child | $30 |
| Infant | Free, with proof of age |
| Additional Platinum cardholder on your account | Not a guest. Enters free on their own card |

Sources disagree on the child age band. The Points Guy says $30 applies from age 2 to 17 and under 2 is free. An October 2026 AwardWallet guide says 3 to 17, with under 3 free. If you travel with a two-year-old, ask at the desk.

The limit is two guests per visit. That means a family of four cannot all enter on one card: the cardholder plus two guests is three people.

No day pass is sold. A person without an eligible card can enter only as someone's guest.

## The same-flight rule

Since July 8, 2026, guests must be traveling on the same flight as the cardholder. AwardWallet quotes the Amex rule: "Card Member guests must be traveling on the same flight as the primary Card Member". It applies at US lounges and at the London, Tokyo Haneda and Hong Kong lounges. A friend flying another airline from the same terminal can no longer come in with you.

## Rules that apply to you and your guests

- You need the card, a government ID and a same-day confirmed boarding pass.
- Entry is allowed within 3 hours of your scheduled departure.
- On a connection, you may enter up to 5 hours before the onward flight.
- There is no entry on arrival, unless you are connecting.

Lounges can also be full. See [the occasional flyer page](/amex-platinum-worth-it-occasional-flyer/) for how the lounge network fits a light travel year.

## When guests are free

Spend $75,000 in eligible purchases on the card in a calendar year, and up to two guests per visit become free. The free access lasts for the rest of that year, all of the following year, and until January 31 of the year after that. Someone who reaches $75,000 during 2026 keeps it through January 31, 2028.

Two details are not confirmed by the sources checked: whether purchases on additional cards count toward the $75,000, and whether an additional cardholder also gets free guests once the account qualifies.

## The other route: an additional card

An additional Platinum card costs $195 a year. Its holder gets their own Centurion Lounge entry, with you or alone, and no guest fee. Compared with a $50 adult guest fee, the card costs less from the fourth visit in a year:

| Visits a year with the same adult | Guest fees | Additional card |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | $100 | $195 |
| 3 | $150 | $195 |
| 4 | $200 | $195 |
| 6 | $300 | $195 |

The additional card also brings other lounge access and hotel status, which the guest fee does not. The no-fee Companion Platinum Card does not include lounge access. Details are on [the authorized user page](/amex-platinum-authorized-user-worth-195/).

## Other lounges treat guests differently

The Centurion fee does not apply across the whole Platinum lounge list. Priority Pass lounges and Escape Lounges allow two free guests where the lounge takes guests. Delta Sky Club has its own guest price, and sources disagree on it: The Points Guy says $50, Upgraded Points says $29.

Some Centurion Lounges outside the US, such as Sydney, Mexico City and Delhi, have their own guest rules.

## Who should skip it

Do not count Centurion Lounge access as a family or couple benefit if:

- You usually travel with a partner or children and will not add them as cardholders. Each visit then costs $30 to $100 in guest fees.
- Your group is larger than three. One card cannot bring everyone in.
- Your home airport has no Centurion Lounge. There were 16 in the US in August 2026.
- Your travel companions are often on different flights.

## Quick answers

**How much is a Centurion Lounge guest with the Amex Platinum?**
$50 per adult and $30 per child at US lounges, for up to two guests per visit.

**How do you get free guests?**
Spend $75,000 in eligible purchases on the card in a calendar year. Then up to two guests per visit are free through January 31 two years later.

**Can a guest be on a different flight?**
No. Since July 8, 2026, guests must be on the same flight as the cardholder.

## Sources

- [The Points Guy: Amex Platinum lounge access](https://thepointsguy.com/credit-cards/american-express-platinum-lounge-access/)
- [AwardWallet: Centurion Lounge guest policy](https://awardwallet.com/credit-cards/centurion-lounge-guest-policy/)
- [AwardWallet: Amex Platinum card page](https://awardwallet.com/credit-cards/amex-membership-rewards/amex-platinum/)
- [The Points Guy: authorized users on the Amex Platinum](https://thepointsguy.com/guide/why-add-authorized-users-amex-platinum/)
- [Upgraded Points: Amex Platinum benefits](https://upgradedpoints.com/credit-cards/reviews/american-express-platinum-card/benefits/)

# What are the Amex Platinum credits really worth if you only count the ones you would use anyway?

Source: https://itsworththefee.com/amex-platinum-credits-real-value/
Facts checked: 2026-11-22
Publisher: Worth the Fee (independent; some pages end with a disclosed referral link)

The 11 main yearly credits on the Amex Platinum add up to $2,994 on paper, against an annual fee of $895. What they are worth to you is smaller: only the credits for things you would have bought anyway count, and for many people that is a few hundred dollars to about $1,300.

This page is information, not financial advice.

## Every credit, as of November 2026

All amounts are "up to". Pieces you do not use in a month, quarter or half-year are lost.

| Credit | Per year | How it is paid | Enrollment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hotel (prepaid Fine Hotels + Resorts, The Hotel Collection or Airbnb Luxe through Amex Travel) | $600 | $300 each half-year | Not stated |
| Resy restaurants | $400 | $100 per quarter | Required |
| Digital entertainment (streaming) | $300 | $25 per month | Required |
| lululemon | $300 | $75 per quarter | Required |
| Equinox membership | $300 | Yearly | Required |
| CLEAR+ membership | $219 | Yearly | Sources differ |
| Airline incidental fees | $200 | Yearly, one airline you pick | Pick the airline first |
| Uber Cash | $200 | $15 per month, plus $20 extra in December | Add the card in the Uber app |
| Oura ring | $200 | Yearly, hardware only | Required |
| Walmart+ membership | $155 | $12.95 per month plus tax | Required |
| Uber One membership | $120 | Yearly | Sources differ |
| Global Entry or TSA PreCheck | $120 or up to $85 | Once every 4 years | Not required |
| SoulCycle at-home bike | $300 per bike | Per purchase | Needs Equinox+ |

Three notes on this list:

- The Saks Fifth Avenue credit ended. Its last day was June 30, 2026.
- From January 1, 2027, Fine Hotels + Resorts bookings need a two-night minimum to earn the hotel credit. The Hotel Collection and Airbnb Luxe already need two nights.
- The airline credit covers fees such as checked bags on one airline you choose. It does not cover tickets.

Review sites quote different totals, from about $3,324 to $3,574, because they count different credits. The first 11 rows above sum to $2,994.

## Why the paper value overstates it

A credit is only worth its face value if you would buy the thing anyway, in the pieces the credit comes in, and you remember to enroll and use each piece. $100 a quarter at Resy restaurants is four separate dinners, not one $400 dinner. A $219 CLEAR+ credit is worth $0 to someone who would never pay for CLEAR+.

## A simple way to add up your own number

Go down the table and give each credit one of three scores:

| Your answer | Count it as |
|---|---|
| I already pay for this, in these amounts | Full value |
| I would use it sometimes, or pay less for it on my own | Half value |
| I would not buy this without the credit | $0 |

Add the column. Then subtract $895. Above zero, the credits alone cover the fee. Below zero, the gap is what you pay for lounges, status and travel protections.

### Two worked examples

| Credit | Reader A (travels, uses Uber and streaming) | Reader B (few habits match) |
|---|---|---|
| Hotel | $600 | $300 (one stay) |
| Airline fees | $200 | $200 |
| Uber Cash | $200 | $0 |
| Digital entertainment | $300 | half: $150 |
| Everything else | $0 | $0 |
| **Total** | **$1,300** | **$650** |
| **After the $895 fee** | **$405 ahead** | **$245 short** |

Reader A is ahead before any lounge visit. Reader B pays $245 a year for lounges and status.

## Who should not count on the credits

- People who dislike tracking. Six of these credits come in monthly, quarterly or half-year pieces.
- People who rarely stay in higher-end hotels. The hotel credit only works at hotels in Amex's two programs.
- People who would shop at lululemon, join Equinox or buy an Oura ring only because of the credit.
- Authorized users expecting their own credits. An additional Platinum card costs $195 a year and has no second set of credits.

## Quick answers

**What is the total value of the Amex Platinum credits?**
The 11 main yearly credits total $2,994 on paper. Sites that add the SoulCycle and Global Entry credits quote totals up to about $3,574.

**Do unused credits roll over?**
No. A monthly, quarterly or half-year piece you do not use is gone.

**Is the Saks credit still on the card?**
No. It ended after June 30, 2026.

## Sources

- [American Express: Platinum Card](https://www.americanexpress.com/us/credit-cards/card/platinum/)
- [American Express: the $600 hotel credit](https://www.americanexpress.com/en-us/travel/get-inspired/Platinum-Card-600-Dollar-Hotel-Credit)
- [The Points Guy: Amex Platinum review](https://thepointsguy.com/credit-cards/reviews/amex-platinum-review/)
- [One Mile at a Time: Amex Platinum review](https://onemileatatime.com/news/amex-platinum-digital-entertainment-credit-improved/)
- [Upgraded Points: Amex Platinum benefits](https://upgradedpoints.com/credit-cards/reviews/american-express-platinum-card/benefits/)
